scenes.headline: How a pure RNN language model keeps its memory
scenes.sub: RWKV-7: a delta-rule state per head, and no growing cache
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Chikki! This model has no attention cache. All it remembers lives in one fixed block of numbers. Here's how that works.

scenes.text: Every head keeps one 64 by 64 matrix. Each token decays it, erases what its key held, and writes a new value.
scenes.say: The idea: every head keeps one sixty-four by sixty-four matrix. Each token fades it, erases what its key held, and writes a new value.

scenes.title: One token through a time-mix layer

steps.say: Each layer first blends the current token with the previous one.
That blend becomes a query called receptance, a decay, a key, a value and a learning rate.
Decay, key, value and learning rate update the state, one matrix per head.
The receptance reads the state, and the result moves up the stack. Only the state carries forward.

scenes.title: The update, per head
scenes.text: S' = S*w - a*(S k) k^T + v k^T

parts.say: First, each column of the state is scaled by its own decay, between about a half and one.
Then it reads what the key already holds and subtracts it, at a learned rate per channel. That's the delta rule.
Then it writes the new value at the key. An overwrite replaces, instead of piling on.

scenes.title: The paper's picture of one head

steps.say: The paper draws it as a four by four toy: decay, minus the erase, plus the write.

scenes.label: state numbers in the 13.3B model: 61 layers, 64 heads, 64 by 64 each
scenes.say: Sixty-one layers, sixty-four heads, sixty-four by sixty-four each. About sixteen million numbers. The post's figure is right.

left.title: Transformer KV cache
left.say: A transformer keeps every key and value. Lossless, but it grows with every token.

right.title: RWKV-7 state
items: 31.5 MiB in fp16, at any length
right.say: The state never grows, so hundreds of conversations fit on one card. The price: overlapping keys interfere, and recall fades.

scenes.text: The whole memory is a fixed set of small matrices: cheap to serve and easy to snapshot, but lossy by design.
scenes.say: So the memory is a fixed set of small matrices: cheap to serve, easy to inspect, lossy by design. Safer? That is still an open experiment.

recap: Each token decays, erases, then writes
About sixteen million numbers, at any length
Constant memory is not perfect recall
scenes.say: Decay, erase, write. A fixed state, not a growing cache.
